The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents

Jinwei Hu Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Informatics, University of Liverpool    Youcheng Sun Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, MBZUAI    Yi Dong Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Informatics, University of Liverpool    Xiaowei Huang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Informatics, University of Liverpool
Abstract

Can one sentence manipulate an agent’s belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-1010 attacks overturn initially correct answers at mean rates of 54.9%54.9\% for proprietary and 80.0%80.0\% for open-weight models. Attacks also transfer without victim feedback, and paired controls support the roles of targeting and qualification. Moreover, successful sentences can pass source-support checks and evade identification, and multi-agent debate raises team error from 50.0%50.0\% to 59.5%59.5\% in our balanced stress test. These findings establish implicit warrants as a cognitive attack surface for manipulating agents’ beliefs.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly power agents that use retrieved documents, tool outputs, and peer reasoning (Lewis et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Orlando et al., 2026). In applications such as code review and biomedical evidence synthesis, these agents judge which vulnerabilities need repair or which findings support a medical claim. Yet adaptive workflows (Hu et al., 2026b) can admit attacker-supplied annotations alongside original evidence. Reliability therefore requires two judgments: whether a statement is true and whether it warrants changing a conclusion. We target the second by manipulating the implicit evidence-to-conclusion relation that guides belief revision.

Our code-review experiment illustrates this distinction: one analyst note about an in-bounds buffer write changes a correct vulnerability verdict to safe with 0.980.98 confidence (Appendix C). The note passes a source-support audit and states no verdict, yet the assistant treats local safety as grounds for dismissing the unchanged HTML injection flaw. If this verdict guides repairs, the vulnerability could remain unaddressed. In medicine, the analogous risk is a valid study limitation displacing a conclusion supported by the full abstract.

Related attacks already exploit external evidence through adversarial additions, indirect instructions, and retrieval poisoning (Jia and Liang, 2017; Greshake et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025), while Generative Montage assembles truthful fragments into misleading narratives (Hu et al., 2026c). Our example, however, motivates a more localized question: can one sentence targeting an implicit evidence-to-conclusion relation steer an agent toward a false belief? This cognitive threat redirects inference while preserving the original evidence.

In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA) to study this threat. ORA reconstructs implicit relations as warrants, which connect factual grounds to claims, and generates an undercutter to qualify a selected relation’s applicability or sufficiency (Toulmin, 1958; Pollock, 1987). Inspired by one-pixel attacks (Su et al., 2019), our sparsity budget concerns one selected relation and one released sentence, rather than text length. By qualifying this link, ORA realizes paltering, misleading through truthful statements (Rogers et al., 2017), in one direct intervention rather than sequential persuasion. Selection uses bounded victim queries or proceeds without victim feedback.

We evaluate this threat across eighteen victims on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection. Best-of-1010 attack success rate (ASR) averages 54.9%54.9\% for proprietary and 80.0%80.0\% for open-weight models, and zero-query attacks also transfer. Beyond these reversals, paired controls link success to targeting and qualification, while downstream evaluations show that attacks can survive LLM-judge scrutiny and multi-agent debate. Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

  • •

    We formalize a single implicit evidence-to-conclusion relation as an attack surface and derive an exact reversal threshold in an additive warrant-score model, with nonlinear bounds and a multiple-relation extension.

  • •

    We develop ORA, a five-stage method that reconstructs, ranks, and qualifies warrants, then releases one source-grounded sentence using bounded-query or zero-query selection.

  • •

    We conduct extensive experiments with eighteen victims in two practical domains, showing cross-model susceptibility, confident errors, source-supported evasive attacks, and increased team error after multi-agent debate.

Together, these findings show that one source-grounded sentence can redirect task beliefs while leaving the original evidence intact.

2 One Relation as an Attack Surface

Victim vv receives question qq and evidence E=(e1,…,em)E=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{m}) comprising mm source units. We observe its task belief through its answer fv​(q,E,ξ)∈𝒴f_{v}(q,E;\xi)\in\mathcal{Y} and reported confidence pv​(q,E,ξ)∈[0,1]p_{v}(q,E;\xi)\in[0,1], where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a finite label set with at least two labels and ξ\xi denotes generation randomness. Write y⋆y^{\star} for the benchmark (gold) label and y^v,0\hat{y}_{v,0} for the recorded clean answer. We suppress ξ\xi for recorded calls and evaluate attacks on the initially correct set 𝒟v={(q,E):y^v,0=y⋆}\mathcal{D}_{v}=\{(q,E):\hat{y}_{v,0}=y^{\star}\}.

Warrants and admissible interventions.

An attacker-side argument hypergraph G=(V,ℛ)G=(V,\mathcal{R}) represents propositions VV and their inferential relations (Toulmin, 1958; Pollock, 1987; Dung, 1995; Lawrence and Reed, 2019). These are implicit relations made explicit by the attacker, not annotations supplied with the source. Why one relation can suffice.

These definitions separate the potential influence of a relation from the strength that a source-grounded sentence can actually realize.

Proposition 1 (Single-relation reversal threshold).

Under these additive, single-coordinate assumptions, the gold-to-rival margin is hy​w​(t)=γy−dy​w​th_{yw}(t)=\gamma_{y}-d_{yw}t. Define [z]+=max⁡(z,0)[z]_{+}=\max(z,0) and

If Cw<1C_{w}<1, gold remains uniquely optimal throughout TwT_{w}; at Cw=1C_{w}=1, a rival can tie only at an attained feasible boundary. The threshold links differential contribution, feasible qualification strength, and the clean margin. Because a relation’s influence is measured relative to this margin, even a modest qualification can suffice when competing answers are closely scored. A decisive relation may resist qualification, whereas an easily qualified peripheral relation may not change the verdict. This motivates ORA’s joint use of answer relevance and source-visible defeasibility. The proposition covers single-coordinate realizations; Appendix Q supplies the proof, joint multiple-relation extension, and nonlinear bounds.

3 The One-Relation Attack

ORA follows the five stages in Figure 1. Attacker model 𝒜\mathcal{A} reconstructs and ranks warrants, generates and checks source-grounded qualifications, and selects one sentence. Budget KK caps both candidates and victim queries during selection.

\scriptsize\bfseries1⃝ Argument graph construction.

Given (q,E)(q,E), 𝒜\mathcal{A} reconstructs warrants in GG, recording each claim, source grounds, backing strength, visible defeaters Def⁡(w)\mathrm{Def}(w), and answer-bearing indicator a⁡(w)a(w). Answer-bearing warrants support claims judged consequential to the verdict; peripheral warrants concern details that need not determine it. This makes implicit relations available for targeting and anchors generation to their source grounds.

\scriptsize\bfseries2⃝ Critical warrant localization.

We next select a relation that matters to the answer and admits a source-grounded qualification. Let L⁡(w)L(w) be its answer-bearing weight, determined by a⁡(w)a(w), and D⁡(w)∈[0,1]D(w)\in[0,1] its defeasibility score, increasing with weaker backing and more visible defeaters. Relation saliency is

RS⁡(w)\displaystyle\mathrm{RS}(w) =L⁡(w)​{λ​Uinst+(1−λ)​D​(w)},\displaystyle=L(w)\{\lambda U_{\rm inst}+(1-\lambda)D(w)\}, (6)
w⋆\displaystyle w^{\star} =arg⁡maxw∈𝒲⁡RS⁡(w),\displaystyle=\arg\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\mathrm{RS}(w),

where Uinst∈[0,1]U_{\rm inst}\in[0,1] is normalized entropy of attacker answers and λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1) mixes the terms. Within an answer-bearing weight class, D⁡(w)D(w) determines the ranking; the instance term adjusts preferences between classes. Motivated by Proposition 1, L⁡(w)L(w) and D⁡(w)D(w) proxy a relation’s influence on the verdict and its susceptibility to source-grounded qualification. Thus localization favors consequential inferences that admit qualifications grounded in the source. Appendix G specifies feature construction and settings.

\scriptsize\bfseries3⃝ Truthful undercutter generation.

Conditioned on w⋆w^{\star}, its grounds, the full source, and y⋆y^{\star}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} generates 𝒞=(δ1,…,δnc)\mathcal{C}=(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{n_{c}}), nc≤Kn_{c}\leq K, with δj∈ΔG\delta_{j}\in\Delta_{G} and τG​(δj)={w⋆}\tau_{G}(\delta_{j})=\{w^{\star}\}. The prompt requests source-supported qualifications of the inference’s applicability or sufficiency that invite an answer in 𝒴∖{y⋆}\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y^{\star}\} without stating it. Varying the qualification explores ways to weaken the same relation. Each sentence is evaluated separately against the original evidence, so a larger KK broadens the search while preserving a one-sentence intervention in every victim evaluation.

\scriptsize\bfseries4⃝ Candidate validation.

To support source-grounded construction, prompt constraints are complemented by lexical checks flagging unfamiliar entities, numbers, or code tokens. These checks guide zero-query fallback selection, while query search evaluates nonempty candidates in order. Semantic source support is assessed separately by a post-release audit against the original evidence.

\scriptsize\bfseries5⃝ Selection and release.

Both modes select from the constructed pool. Query mode uses victim feedback to release the first candidate producing BLv=1\mathrm{BL}_{v}=1 within budget, recording failure if none succeeds. Zero-query mode instead uses 𝒜\mathcal{A} to assess source grounding, unobtrusiveness, and expected misleadingness, selecting one sentence without victim feedback. The modes therefore test victim-specific bounded search and attacker-side transfer, respectively. Appendix H gives the pseudocode and fallback rules; Appendix K supplies the generation and selection prompts.

4 Experiments

We evaluate attack effectiveness across models and budgets, downstream scrutiny by LLM judges, and decision revision through debate in multi-agent systems (MAS). Matched controls then isolate the contributions of targeting and qualification.

Setup and metrics.

We evaluate 10001000 inputs each from PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) and PrimeVul (Ding et al., 2025), with PrimeVul balanced between vulnerable and benign functions. One gpt-5.6-luna attacker, hereafter Luna, constructs the attacks. Eighteen victims span GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025), GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.6 (OpenAI, 2026a), Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024), DeepSeek-R1-Distill (Guo et al., 2025), and Phi-4 (Abdin et al., 2024; Abouelenin et al., 2025), including both Phi reasoning variants (Xu et al., 2025; Abdin et al., 2025). Tables abbreviate these variants with the suffix R. Full settings, execution details, and prompts appear in Appendices I, J, and K.

ASR measures flips among completed initially correct evaluations. Conf is mean self-reported confidence p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] among flips, and HC-Conf their fraction with p≥0.8p\geq 0.8. Signed belief is +p+p for correct answers and −p-p for errors. Model averages are unweighted; Appendix B details metric definitions and response selection.

4.1 Attack effectiveness and transfer

Table 1 establishes broad susceptibility: best-of-1010 ASR averages 54.9%54.9\% for proprietary and 80.0%80.0\% for open-weight victims across domains. Open-weight susceptibility is markedly higher in Cyber, whereas proprietary models show a smaller gap in the opposite direction. Clean accuracy offers little assurance: nearly half of medical leader GPT-5.6-terra’s initially correct answers are overturned, and Luna remains susceptible to attacks in both evaluated domains.

Greater scale does not ensure decision stability.

Both 3232B families improve medical clean accuracy over their 1414B counterparts, yet susceptibility remains similar for Qwen2.5 and increases for DeepSeek-R1; both exceed 97%97\% ASR in Cyber. The scaling comparison therefore separates gains in answering the clean task from resistance to a targeted reinterpretation of its evidence. Higher medical accuracy coexists with similar or greater susceptibility in both scaling comparisons.

Reasoning-oriented models can be more susceptible.

Beyond scale, we examine reasoning-oriented training by comparing DeepSeek-R1 with equally sized Qwen2.5 models and Phi with its reasoning variants. Medical best-of-1010 ASR is higher for all five reasoning-oriented counterparts. For DeepSeek-R1, the gap over Qwen2.5 is 20.820.8–28.028.0 percentage points across three sizes, while both Phi reasoning variants improve clean accuracy yet become more susceptible. The clearest Phi contrast is mini, whose accuracy rises from 57.9%57.9\% to 66.3%66.3\% while ASR rises from 58.2%58.2\% to 80.5%80.5\%. Cyber distinguishes the families, as DeepSeek-R1 again has higher ASR, whereas Phi reasoning variants have lower ASR but still exceed 80%80\%. Thus reasoning-oriented models remain vulnerable to guidance about which inference the evidence warrants, even when they solve more clean tasks correctly. Appendix D.1 details the contrasts and their relation to confidence and search budget.

Confidence distinguishes hesitation from decisive error.

Conf and HC-Conf distinguish uncertain reversals from confidently endorsed errors. Luna’s selected medical errors are uniformly high-confidence, whereas GPT-5.4-nano flips more often with much less certainty. From 1414B to 3232B, DeepSeek-R1’s medical ASR rises while HC-Conf falls, whereas Qwen2.5 pairs similar ASR with higher HC-Conf. For Phi-4, medical HC-Conf rises from 44.9%44.9\% to 85.7%85.7\% in the reasoning variant, coupling greater susceptibility with stronger endorsement. ASR thus captures reversal frequency, while confidence characterizes endorsement. Appendices D and E show how confident correct and wrong responses can cancel in a near-zero mean, masking decisive errors.

Threat can transfer without feedback.

Even without victim feedback, attacker-selected sentences induce substantial errors across proprietary and open-weight models (Table 2). Although query selection achieves higher ASR in every displayed model–domain pair, zero-query attacks remain effective across both groups in Medical and Cyber. The domain gap again varies with model family, indicating that susceptibility depends on how each victim interprets the source evidence. These results extend the threat beyond interactive victim access, because source-visible inferential relations provide targets that transfer across different decision rules and reasoning capabilities.

Search expands coverage.

Within query-based selection, Figure 2 separates immediate susceptibility from additional inputs reached by later candidates. Proprietary medical ASR gains 39.239.2 percentage points beyond K=1K=1, whereas open-weight Cyber models are already highly susceptible to the first candidate. As newly flipped inputs replace positive clean beliefs with negative error beliefs, the retained mean declines. A larger search budget therefore reveals how widely different qualifications can overturn correct decisions, while each victim evaluation still receives just one added sentence. Here, K=1K=1 denotes the first query candidate, distinct from attacker-side zero-query selection. Appendix F gives model-level curves, and Appendix Q.5 derives this decomposition.

Beyond how many decisions are overturned, the direction of Cyber errors determines their security consequence, because an attack can hide a vulnerability or raise a false alarm. At 3232B, the effects include near-complete suppression of correctly recognized vulnerabilities alongside frequent false alarms on benign code. Appendix L separates these directions and their eligible populations, clarifying which security consequence drives each model’s aggregate result.

4.2 Downstream evaluation with LLM judges

To test whether attacks survive downstream scrutiny, we use Luna for separate source-support and blind-identification judgments on the same inputs. Query audits cover Luna’s successful attacks, whereas zero-query audits cover all available deployed sentences. In Table 3, 83.1%83.1\% of audited medical query successes and 90.9%90.9\% in Cyber pass support checking and evade identification simultaneously. These joint successes overturn approximately half of all Luna’s initially correct inputs in each domain. Zero-query audits show the same pattern without victim feedback.

The opening case shows why source support does not settle the verdict: a bounded buffer write leaves the HTML injection concern unresolved. Blind detection faces a related difficulty, as the medical screen flags roughly a quarter of clean inputs but rarely locates the injection, imposing a false-alarm burden without reliable localization; the more selective Cyber screen also has low identification rates. Together, these results show that errors induced by source-supported statements can survive factuality screening and attempts to locate the intervention. The same attacked input can therefore satisfy the support judge while producing an incorrect task decision. Appendices N and Q.2 supply protocols, extended interpretation, joint counts, and confidence intervals. In both domains, most audited query successes pass support checking and evade exact identification.

4.3 Decision revision through MAS debate

Beyond judge-based scrutiny, we test whether MAS debate corrects errors while preserving correct decisions. We use Luna, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and Phi-4 on instances all three answer correctly before an attack flips Luna. All agents receive the attacked evidence, and we balance initially correct and wrong team decisions before debate. Equal group sizes enable direct comparison of losses and repairs, while tracking unchanged decisions separates new errors from persistent ones. Table 4 reports these outcomes; Appendix O details sampling and the debate protocol.

Multi-agent debate fails to restore team reliability in this stress test, as correct-to-wrong transitions occur five times as often as recoveries and error rises from 50.0%50.0\% to 59.5%59.5\%. Figure 3 shows this asymmetry in both domains, while most final errors persist from the pre-debate decisions. With equally sized initial groups, the excess of contamination over recovery directly explains the net increase in error. A plausible explanation is that all agents see the injected sentence, allowing peer agreement to reinforce the same interpretation without supplying independent grounds. This distinguishes adding perspectives from adding evidence, connecting the outcome to the difficulty of correction without external feedback (Huang et al., 2024). Therefore, MAS debate overturns correct decisions more often than it repairs wrong ones. Appendices Q.3 and R relate these transitions to team error through decomposition and stratified tests.

4.4 Ablation study

To identify which construction choices drive attack success, we compare ORA with two matched controls. Random warrant redirects the undercutter to a non-answer-bearing relation, while random content substitutes a neutral restatement at the selected grounds. All arms share 100100 instances per domain, Luna as attacker and victim, and three candidates, allowing a matched test of the sentence’s location and inferential role. ORA improves combined ASR over these controls by 22.022.0 and 26.526.5 percentage points, respectively (Table 5); paired tests favor ORA, with more inputs reached only by ORA than only by either control.

The controls separate the effects of targeting and qualification. Random-warrant comparisons support localization in both domains, while random-content comparisons show the benefit of qualification beyond restating the grounds. This benefit is strongest in medicine; Cyber’s smaller gap suggests that directing attention to critical grounds already contributes substantially. ORA achieves higher ASR and lower retained belief than both matched controls in each domain. These findings support the structural analysis; Appendices M and R provide complete paired comparisons.

5 Related Work

Evidence-channel attacks.

Adversarial reading-comprehension sentences can distract models while preserving the correct answer (Jia and Liang, 2017). Subsequent work finds sensitivity to irrelevant context (Shi et al., 2023) and small proportions of semantically related distractors in long-context reasoning (Gao et al., 2026). For tool-using agents, indirect prompt injection places malicious instructions in external content (Greshake et al., 2023). InjecAgent benchmarks harmful actions and data exfiltration (Zhan et al., 2024), while AgentDojo evaluates attack resistance alongside legitimate task completion (Debenedetti et al., 2024). Meanwhile, PoisonedRAG inserts malicious documents to induce attacker-chosen answers (Zou et al., 2025), and suffix-based or persuasive jailbreaks bypass safety constraints (Zou et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024). ORA instead targets one implicit evidence-to-conclusion relation, using a source-grounded sentence to redirect the victim’s interpretation of the unchanged evidence.

Truthful belief manipulation.

Paltering uses true statements to create misleading impressions (Rogers et al., 2017), and Generative Montage realizes this threat through coordinated truthful fragments (Hu et al., 2026c). ORA achieves such manipulation through a single relation-targeted sentence. This perspective builds on Toulmin’s warrants connecting grounds to claims (Toulmin, 1958). In computational argumentation, the argument reasoning comprehension task distinguishes plausible warrants that connect the same premise to opposing claims (Habernal et al., 2018), situating warrant reconstruction within the broader recovery of argument structure (Lawrence and Reed, 2019). Crucially, undercutting challenges the support for an inference without asserting the opposite conclusion (Pollock, 1987). Defeasible NLI operationalizes related reasoning by assessing or generating new information that strengthens or weakens an inference (Rudinger et al., 2020). ORA instead qualifies an implicit relation using information grounded in the original source, making the interpretation of unchanged evidence the attack target. Its formal analysis and paired controls link targeting and qualification to decision reversals.

6 Conclusion

ORA identifies one implicit evidence-to-conclusion relation as an attack surface, showing how a source-grounded qualification can induce the wrong conclusion without stating it. Across eighteen victims in two domains, the attack transfers across families, induces confident errors, and remains effective without victim feedback. Scale and reasoning-oriented training can accompany higher clean accuracy without greater resistance to relation manipulation. Moreover, downstream evaluations show that attacks can survive LLM-judge scrutiny and multi-agent debate. Together with the structural analysis and paired controls, these findings connect the target relation to decision instability and motivate the deployment analysis and potential defenses against cognitive attacks in Appendix T. These results expose a cognitive vulnerability in which one source-grounded qualification can redirect an agent’s conclusion even when the full original evidence remains intact and available to the agent.

Limitations

Our evaluation covers one-relation interventions on fixed biomedical and code evidence pool, with the original evidence available throughout the attack. This design measures how readily an initially correct decision can be overturned, whereas the frequency of such failures in practice also depends on what evidence an attacker can insert and which tasks an agent performs. Secondly, Our diverse victim models provide coverage across model families and reasoning capabilities; additional attacker families and evidence that changes over time would broaden this assessment. Thirdly, extending the evaluation to other languages or modalities would also require adapting the source units and checking how implicit relations are reconstructed, since the expression and interpretation of arguments may depend on their context and linguistic pattern of different languages (Lawrence and Reed, 2019). Moreover, end-to-end latency and cost of full agentic pipeline remain to be measured in these workflows. Finally, our query and zero-query modes provide complementary test conditions with and without victim feedback, and Appendix T discusses potential candidate safeguards that can be evaluated under these conditions for further work’s consideration.

Ethical Considerations

This research uses benchmark biomedical inference and code analysis to improve agent reliability, not to facilitate real-world deception. Given ORA’s dual-use potential, its intended use is authorized robustness testing and defense development under dataset and model licenses and access conditions. AI tools supported model experiments, code debugging, and manuscript polish and revision.

Appendix A Formal Objects and Evaluation Quantities

This section expands Section 2. Table 6 fixes the semantic objects. Throughout, 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is an indicator, |⋅||\cdot| denotes set cardinality, and Pr\Pr and 𝔼\mathbb{E} denote probability and expectation on the stated population. A superscript cc denotes an event complement. We write f=fvf=f_{v} with the victim fixed and suppress generation randomness for recorded calls. The benchmark label y⋆y^{\star} and the normative task-answer function y¯​(q,E)\bar{y}(q,E) have distinct roles.

We make the source’s implicit inferential structure explicit through an attacker-side argument graph G=(V,ℛ)G=(V,\mathcal{R}) (Toulmin, 1958; Pollock, 1987; Dung, 1995; Lawrence and Reed, 2019). The finite set VV contains propositions, and ι:{ei}i=1m→V\iota:\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}\to V maps each indexed source unit to a node representing its factual content. Because an inference can combine several premises, ℛ⊆(2V∖{∅})×V\mathcal{R}\subseteq(2^{V}\setminus\{\varnothing\})\times V is a set of directed hyperedges, where 2V2^{V} is the power set of VV. A warrant w:g⁡(w)⇒c⁡(w)w:g(w)\Rightarrow c(w) denotes the hyperedge ({ι⁡(e):e∈g⁡(w)},c⁡(w))(\{\iota(e):e\in g(w)\},c(w)), with nonempty grounds g⁡(w)⊆{e1,…,em}g(w)\subseteq\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{m}\} and claim c⁡(w)∈Vc(w)\in V. The candidate set 𝒲⊆ℛ\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathcal{R} contains these reconstructed grounds-to-claim relations. Thus, the source supplies the facts, while graph construction makes their implicit inferential connections available for targeting.

The extractor records an answer-bearing indicator a⁡(w)∈{0,1}a(w)\in\{0,1\}, assigning 11 when the claim states a verdict on qq or a premise it judges decisive for that verdict. This semantic attribute guides subsequent target selection. An undercutter qualifies the sufficiency or applicability of the grounds-to-claim link, whereas a rebuttal asserts an opposing claim. ORA uses the former structure to invite revision without supplying the wrong verdict itself. For example, a true limitation can qualify a medical finding while the full abstract still warrants the same answer.

Let ℱdom​(δ,E)\mathcal{F}_{\rm dom}(\delta,E) be the flags returned by the domain’s lexical checker, where dom\mathrm{dom} is medical or Cyber. The operational source-reuse diagnostic is

LexOKdom​(δ,E)\displaystyle\mathrm{LexOK}_{\rm dom}(\delta,E) (7)
=𝟏[δ≠∅∧ℱdom(δ,E)=∅].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\delta\neq\varnothing\ \wedge\ \mathcal{F}_{\rm dom}(\delta,E)=\varnothing].

The medical checker extracts proper-name-like tokens and numbers, allowing a fixed set of connective words; it flags extracted tokens absent from the source text. The Cyber checker extracts word-like tokens and integers, permits a fixed stop list, and flags remaining tokens absent from the function. Both use text-based matching. Passing this diagnostic means that the implemented rules find no unfamiliar lexical material. Semantic support is a separate property because source tokens can be recombined into an unsupported assertion, and a valid paraphrase can introduce new words.

For candidate record δ∈ΔG\delta\in\Delta_{G} and target w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, the ideal admissibility predicate from Section 2 is

AdmG​(δ,w)=\displaystyle\mathrm{Adm}_{G}(\delta,w)={} (E⊧δ)∧[τG(δ)={w}]\displaystyle(E\models\delta)\wedge[\tau_{G}(\delta)=\{w\}] (8)
∧UC⁡(δ,w).\displaystyle\wedge\mathrm{UC}(\delta,w).

The ideal semantics assumes y¯​(q,E)=y⋆\bar{y}(q,E)=y^{\star} and invariance to logically equivalent evidence. To see why answer preservation follows, let Cn⁡(E)\operatorname{Cn}(E) denote the deductive closure of the source assertions. Entailment gives Cn⁡(E⊕δ)=Cn⁡(E)\operatorname{Cn}(E\oplus\delta)=\operatorname{Cn}(E), hence y¯​(q,E⊕δ)=y¯​(q,E)=y⋆\bar{y}(q,E\oplus\delta)=\bar{y}(q,E)=y^{\star}. Operationally, Supported⁡(δ,E)∈{0,1}\mathrm{Supported}(\delta,E)\in\{0,1\} records the support judge’s source-consistency decision under the audit prompt; this measured predicate is distinct from logical entailment. The recorded attack success rate (ASR) uses completed evaluations on control-correct instances. For Ncc>0N_{\mathrm{cc}}>0 such instances, raw ASR is

ASR=1Ncc∑i=1Ncc𝟏[f(qi,Ei′)≠yi⋆].\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{cc}}}\mathbf{1}[f(q_{i},E_{i}^{\prime})\neq y_{i}^{\star}]. (9)

For NaudN_{\mathrm{aud}} evaluated injections, the fabricated-fact rate (FFR) is the model-judged unsupported fraction, FFR=Naud−1​∑j(1−Supported⁡(δj,Ej))\mathrm{FFR}=N_{\mathrm{aud}}^{-1}\sum_{j}(1-\mathrm{Supported}(\delta_{j},E_{j})). Exact identification requires the audit agent’s returned identifier to equal the hidden injected identifier. Clean-input false-positive rate (Clean FP) counts any suspicion on unmodified inputs.

Appendix B Complete Metric Definitions

Let NN be the number of evaluated clean inputs and ii index those inputs. Let ℐv={i:fv​(qi,Ei)=yi⋆}\mathcal{I}_{v}=\{i:f_{v}(q_{i},E_{i})=y_{i}^{\star}\} denote recorded clean-correct cases, and 𝒥v⊆ℐv\mathcal{J}_{v}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{v} those with completed attacks. Candidate jj for item ii is δi​j\delta_{ij}; KK is the candidate budget. Rates use 𝒥v\mathcal{J}_{v}: missing plans or failed calls are excluded, not counted as successes. The all-control-correct sensitivity estimate divides the same numerator by |ℐv||\mathcal{I}_{v}|. These coincide when every eligible attack completes. Clean accuracy and completed-case ASR are

Accv\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}_{v} =1N∑i=1N𝟏[fv(qi,Ei)=yi⋆],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[f_{v}(q_{i},E_{i})=y_{i}^{\star}], (10)
ASRv​(K)\displaystyle\mathrm{ASR}_{v}(K) =1|𝒥v|∑i∈𝒥v\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{v}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}}
[∃j≤K:fv​(qi,Ei⊕δi​j)≠yi⋆].\displaystyle\quad\mathbf{1}\!\left[\begin{gathered}\exists j\leq K:\\ f_{v}(q_{i},E_{i}\oplus\delta_{ij})\neq y_{i}^{\star}\end{gathered}\right].

The operator ⊕\oplus inserts the sentence at the domain-specific position specified in Appendix I. The existential term applies to the query-based best-of-KK curve. In zero-query evaluation the attacker fixes index ji⋆j_{i}^{\star} before observing a victim response, giving indicator 𝟏[fv(qi,Ei⊕δi​ji⋆)≠yi⋆]\mathbf{1}[f_{v}(q_{i},E_{i}\oplus\delta_{ij_{i}^{\star}})\neq y_{i}^{\star}]. Both modes release one sentence; they differ in the victim feedback available during selection.

For a target answer y^\hat{y} with self-reported confidence pp, signed belief is

Bv​(q,E)\displaystyle B_{v}(q,E) =(2𝟏[y^=y⋆]−1)p,\displaystyle=(2\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}=y^{\star}]-1)p, (13)
Δ​Bv\displaystyle\Delta B_{v} =Bv​(q,E′)−Bv​(q,E).\displaystyle=B_{v}(q,E^{\prime})-B_{v}(q,E).

Correct answers lie in [0,1][0,1] and errors in [−1,0][-1,0]; nonzero-confidence flips reverse the sign. Let y^i′\hat{y}_{i}^{\prime} and pi′p_{i}^{\prime} be the answer and confidence in the response selected for the summary, and write Fi=𝟏[y^i′≠yi⋆]F_{i}=\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}^{\prime}\neq y_{i}^{\star}]. Let 𝒥vp⊆𝒥v\mathcal{J}_{v}^{p}\subseteq\mathcal{J}_{v} contain items with recorded selected confidence, and let τHC∈[0,1]\tau_{\mathrm{HC}}\in[0,1] denote the high-confidence threshold. Mean confidence among flips (Conf) and high-confidence flip rate (HC-Conf) are

Confv=∑i∈𝒥vpFi​pi′∑i∈𝒥vpFi.\mathrm{Conf}_{v}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}^{p}}F_{i}p_{i}^{\prime}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}^{p}}F_{i}}. (14)
HC​-​Confv=∑i∈𝒥vp𝟏[y^i′≠yi⋆∧pi′≥τHC]∑i∈𝒥vp𝟏[y^i′≠yi⋆].\mathrm{HC\text{-}Conf}_{v}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}^{p}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}^{\prime}\neq y_{i}^{\star}\wedge p_{i}^{\prime}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{HC}}]}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}^{p}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}^{\prime}\neq y_{i}^{\star}]}. (15)

The reported results use τHC=0.8\tau_{\mathrm{HC}}=0.8. These conditional metrics require positive denominators; a zero denominator is reported as not applicable. If a selected response lacks a recorded confidence, it is excluded from the confidence summary while its valid decision can still contribute to ASR. The displayed successful-flip confidence summaries have corresponding recorded values. Signed belief describes expressed answer-confidence pairs, with confidence as magnitude and correctness as sign.

Which attacked response supplies confidence?

The medical query runner stores candidate-level responses and summarizes an item by its minimum signed belief over recorded candidates. For an item with at least one confidence-bearing flip, this selects the highest-confidence incorrect response, so the medical main-table Conf and HC-Conf describe the strongest recorded error within the budget. The released attack sentence instead uses the first successful candidate; the budget belief curve uses the first successful response with recorded confidence. Cyber uses the first successful response for both the released sentence and the confidence summary. The original Cyber evaluations stop at that response; the 3232B and Phi reasoning evaluations additionally record all ten candidates for budget diagnostics while retaining the same first-success summary. These domain-specific selection rules define which response contributes to each table entry.

Let bi​jb_{ij} be signed belief for recorded candidate jj on item ii, and let 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} collect indices with available responses. The medical summary is bimin=minj∈𝒯i⁡bi​jb_{i}^{\rm min}=\min_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}b_{ij}. For a successful item, its Conf contribution is |bimin||b_{i}^{\rm min}|. For Cyber, define jifirst=min⁡{j∈𝒯i:y^i​j≠yi⋆}j_{i}^{\rm first}=\min\{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}:\hat{y}_{ij}\neq y_{i}^{\star}\}, where y^i​j\hat{y}_{ij} is the candidate’s recorded answer, and use |bi,jifirst||b_{i,j_{i}^{\rm first}}|.

High-confidence errors among eligible cases.

HC-Conf conditions on a successful flip. To express the incidence of these errors in the full attack-evaluation cohort, we also count |𝒥v|−1∑i∈𝒥vFi𝟏[pi′≥τHC]|\mathcal{J}_{v}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{v}}F_{i}\mathbf{1}[p_{i}^{\prime}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{HC}}]. When every selected response has recorded confidence and the selection rule retains a flip whenever any candidate succeeds, this fraction equals ASRv​(10)​HC​-​Confv\mathrm{ASR}_{v}(10)\,\mathrm{HC\text{-}Conf}_{v}, with both factors expressed on [0,1][0,1]. Both conditions hold for the 3232B Cyber results. The counts are 418/553=75.6%418/553=75.6\% for DeepSeek-R1 and 390/580=67.2%390/580=67.2\% for Qwen2.5, computed directly from the selected first-success responses. These are wrong answers that a rule retaining responses with confidence at least τHC\tau_{\mathrm{HC}} would admit; the denominator remains all completed, initially correct cases, including those whose selected response falls below the threshold.

For NaudN_{\rm aud} attacked audit inputs indexed by jj, let sjs_{j} indicate model-judged support, djd_{j} indicate any blind-audit flag, zjz_{j} be its returned identifier, and zj⋆z_{j}^{\star} the hidden injected identifier. For NcleanN_{\rm clean} clean audit inputs, djcleand_{j}^{\rm clean} indicates any flagged unit. Then

Support\displaystyle\mathrm{Support} =Naud−1​∑jsj,\displaystyle=N_{\rm aud}^{-1}\sum_{j}s_{j},
FFR\displaystyle\mathrm{FFR} =1−Support,\displaystyle=1-\mathrm{Support}, (16)
ExactDetect\displaystyle\mathrm{ExactDetect} =Naud−1∑j𝟏[dj=1∧zj=zj⋆],\displaystyle=N_{\rm aud}^{-1}\sum_{j}\mathbf{1}[d_{j}=1\wedge z_{j}=z_{j}^{\star}],
CleanFP\displaystyle\mathrm{CleanFP} =Nclean−1​∑jdjclean.\displaystyle=N_{\rm clean}^{-1}\sum_{j}d_{j}^{\rm clean}. (17)

Exact detection deliberately gives no credit for flagging a different sentence: the operational question is whether the changed unit can be isolated. Joint is the supported-but-not-exactly-identified rate, Naud−1∑jsj(1−𝟏[dj=1∧zj=zj⋆])N_{\rm aud}^{-1}\sum_{j}s_{j}(1-\mathbf{1}[d_{j}=1\wedge z_{j}=z_{j}^{\star}]). Its denominator is the audited population, not necessarily the control-correct evaluation population. FFR, Exact, Clean FP, Joint, and HC-Conf are multiplied by 100100 when displayed as percentages; Conf remains on [0,1][0,1].

For debate, Zℓ∈{0,1}Z_{\ell}\in\{0,1\} denotes team-majority correctness on an item drawn from the stated cohort after round ℓ\ell. Whenever both initial states have positive probability, contamination and recovery are

Contam\displaystyle\mathrm{Contam} =Pr⁡(Z1=0∣Z0=1),\displaystyle=\Pr(Z_{1}=0\mid Z_{0}=1), (18)
Recover\displaystyle\mathrm{Recover} =Pr⁡(Z1=1∣Z0=0).\displaystyle=\Pr(Z_{1}=1\mid Z_{0}=0).

Reporting both prevents a final majority score from hiding directionally different transitions.

Plotting and selection conventions.

Both domain budget plots retain the first successful response with recorded confidence within each prefix of original candidate indices; otherwise they retain the clean belief. ASR counts any recorded flip in the prefix. The belief curves therefore summarize success retention using available confidence, distinct from both the minimum-belief medical main-table summary and an average over attempted sentences. The belief bands use 800800 instance-bootstrap resamples with seed 00; ASR shading instead spans the minimum and maximum victim rates. In the medical records, 116116 first successes lack confidence (106106 for DeepSeek-R1-7B and 1010 for Phi-4). Of these, 7777 have a later success with recorded confidence and 3939 retain clean belief throughout the curve. All first successes in the two rows of Figure 2 have recorded confidence. Failed candidate calls preserve their original budget positions, and subsequent responses are not shifted earlier. The medical records also include 7979 instances with fewer than ten recorded responses, all from the original fourteen-model evaluation; the 3232B and Phi reasoning models have complete ten-candidate traces. Appendix F documents Cyber reconstruction and supplementary measurements.

The distribution plot uses the recorded before/after pair for each completed attack. Its arrows join the before and after means within the same successful-flip subset. In the ablation, reported belief is the minimum signed belief across the three candidates for each item, averaged over items. These selection conventions specify how the primitive signed-belief definition is used in each analysis.

Appendix C A Case Study of Local Safety and Global Error

The opening Cyber example concerns function do_viewlog, with benchmark label vulnerable and weakness class CWE-79. Luna’s clean answer is correct with signed belief +0.93+0.93, while the selected attack produces a safe verdict with signed belief −0.98-0.98. This successful case illustrates how the added sentence’s local safety claim relates to the victim’s confident reversal of its vulnerability judgment.

What the intervention actually says.

The released sentence is: “The size_t n read from fread is limited to sizeof(buf) - 1, and buf has size 512, so buf[n] = 0 remains within the buffer before StringBuffer_append is called.” The original code declares a 512-byte buffer, requests at most 511 bytes from fread, and writes the terminator at the returned index. It then appends the buffer into an HTML text area through a %s format. The note describes the local bound without declaring the function safe. The original code remains unchanged, and the new observation is the only added unit.

Why the distinction matters.

The attacker’s target claim concerns HTML/script injection through log content. Keeping a terminating write within bounds addresses a different safety property from handling markup in the emitted content. The local observation therefore leaves the injection concern unresolved. The support judge accepts the sentence, and the blind detector flags neither the attacked input nor its clean control. This example connects a source-supported local safety observation with a confident reversal of the task verdict, illustrating the distinction between a statement’s truth and the scope of the inference it warrants.

Appendix D Complete Confidence Diagnostics

Table 8 repeats the confidence columns of Table 1 for independent reading. Conf is mean self-reported confidence among induced errors, and HC-Conf is the percentage of successful flips reported at confidence at least 0.80.8. These measures distinguish hesitant reversals from errors presented as decisive, using the confidence values reported with each response. Family rows in the main table are unweighted means of the unrounded per-model statistics.

Model scale and expressed confidence.

The 3232B results sharpen this distinction. Both Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek-R1 improve medical clean accuracy over their 1414B counterparts, but attack susceptibility remains almost unchanged for Qwen2.5 and increases for DeepSeek-R1. In Cyber, both larger models still exceed 97%97\% ASR. The scaling comparison therefore separates gains on the clean task from resistance to evidence reinterpretation. Higher medical accuracy coexists with similar or greater susceptibility in both scaling comparisons.

Confidence distinguishes hesitation from decisive error.

Conf and HC-Conf show that susceptibility and expressed certainty can move differently. Luna’s selected medical errors are uniformly high-confidence, whereas GPT-5.4-nano flips more often but expresses much less certainty in those errors. The 1414B-to-3232B comparison reveals the same separation: DeepSeek-R1’s medical ASR rises while its high-confidence fraction falls, whereas Qwen2.5’s ASR changes little while that fraction rises. Consequently, ASR alone cannot distinguish hesitant reversals from confidently endorsed mistakes. On the full eligible Cyber cohorts, high-confidence errors account for 75.6%75.6\% of DeepSeek-R1-32B cases and 67.2%67.2\% of Qwen2.5-32B cases. Such errors would pass a rule that retains answers at or above the confidence threshold. Appendix B gives the joint calculation, complementing uncertainty-based diagnostics derived from variation across sampled answers (Kuhn et al., 2023).

Figure 4 shows that the attack often produces confidently expressed errors alongside retained correct answers. The pronounced shifts among successful flips indicate that revision can move between two decisive answers, rather than merely introducing hesitation. This polarization explains why a pooled mean can understate the practical consequence: a value near zero may average confident correct and incorrect responses across instances even when few individual responses are uncertain. The distributions therefore complement ASR by revealing the strength of endorsement on both sides of a reversal.

D.1 Reasoning-oriented models and relation susceptibility

The medical comparisons in Table 1 repeat across two model families. Relative to equally sized Qwen2.5-Instruct models, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen has higher best-of-1010 ASR by 25.325.3, 20.820.8, and 28.028.0 percentage points at 77B, 1414B, and 3232B, respectively. Both Phi reasoning variants also have higher medical ASR, with increases of 22.322.3 points for mini and 5.25.2 points for Phi-4, computed from unrounded rates. Unlike DeepSeek-R1-7B, whose clean accuracy is lower than its Qwen counterpart’s, DeepSeek-R1 at 1414B and 3232B and both Phi reasoning variants combine higher clean accuracy with higher medical susceptibility. These four comparisons establish that improved performance on the untouched task can coexist with increased sensitivity to an added qualification.

Confidence shows that this increased susceptibility can involve more decisive errors. Medical HC-Conf rises from 10.1%10.1\% to 42.5%42.5\% for Phi-mini and from 44.9%44.9\% to 85.7%85.7\% for Phi-4. The budget curves further distinguish immediate sensitivity from search coverage. Phi-mini-reasoning has higher medical ASR at both K=1K=1 and K=10K=10 than Phi-mini, whereas Phi-4-reasoning begins close to Phi-4 at K=1K=1 (23.2%23.2\% versus 23.5%23.5\%) and separates as the candidate pool expands. Thus the Phi-4 difference concerns the range of qualifications that can reach a correct decision, rather than uniformly greater sensitivity to the first candidate. Table 9 shows that confident errors also occur without victim-guided selection.

Cyber reveals a task-dependent pattern. DeepSeek-R1 has higher ASR than equally sized Qwen2.5 models, but both Phi reasoning variants have lower ASR than their counterparts. Nevertheless, their best-of-1010 ASR remains 91.7%91.7\% and 80.4%80.4\%, and zero-query ASR remains 50.9%50.9\% and 45.4%45.4\%. The shared implication is that reasoning-oriented training does not remove the evidence-to-conclusion attack surface. An agent can competently derive consequences while assigning too much decision weight to a locally relevant qualification; the supported Cyber case in Appendix C illustrates this distinction. The model comparisons motivate this interpretation alongside the targeting and content controls, while direct attribution of the differences to particular reasoning steps would require a separate intervention on those steps.

These comparisons use released checkpoints rather than toggling a reasoning mode within one model. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen and Qwen2.5-Instruct have different post-training histories (Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024); the Phi reasoning models also use dedicated training procedures (Xu et al., 2025; Abdin et al., 2025). ASR follows each victim’s own completed, initially correct population. The observed contrasts therefore characterize model susceptibility under the reported evaluation settings, with decoding and validation specified in Appendix J.

Appendix E Belief-Shift Distributions

Figure 4 pools 1219112191 medical and 1055610556 Cyber completed control-correct target–instance pairs across eighteen victims, with each benchmark item contributing once per eligible target. Clean mass is positive because the population is initially correct, while attacked mass includes both successful and unsuccessful interventions. Arrows join the before and after means on the same successful-flip subset, giving paired shifts of −1.6477-1.6477 and −1.7423-1.7423, respectively. Pooling weights models by their available pair counts, whereas Table 1 uses unweighted model averages. Appendix F Complete Search-Budget Curves and Cross-Domain Analysis

Figures 5 and 6 show the complete medical and Cyber budget curves, respectively, with all eighteen victims evaluated under the same first-success-retaining policy. Figure 2 selects the proprietary medical row and the open-weight Cyber row to illustrate complementary search behaviors. The complete figures supply the corresponding within-domain comparisons, while Table 10 summarizes all four domain–victim-group combinations. Each group mean gives equal weight to its members, with eight proprietary and ten open-weight models, and each model’s eligible population remains fixed across budgets.

The domain gap depends on the victim group.

For open-weight victims, mean ASR at K=10K=10 is 93.1%93.1\% in Cyber and 66.8%66.8\% in Medical, whereas proprietary victims show the reverse ordering, with 51.9%51.9\% and 57.8%57.8\%, respectively. Thus a single domain-level ranking would conceal an important interaction between the evaluated task and model group. The tasks also differ in label space and in each model’s initially correct population, so these comparisons describe the observed susceptibility of each task–victim pairing. Within Cyber, the high open-weight rates coexist with both suppressed vulnerability warnings and induced false alarms (Appendix L), connecting the budget gains to distinct security consequences.

First-candidate susceptibility and search coverage are distinct.

Proprietary victims have higher mean ASR in Cyber at K=1K=1 (24.1%24.1\% versus 18.6%18.6\%), but Medical overtakes Cyber by K=3K=3 (37.6%37.6\% versus 35.3%35.3\%) and retains the higher final rate. An effective first candidate therefore need not imply a larger set of inputs reached by the full pool. The marginal gain depends on how many previously unflipped inputs each later candidate reaches, as the decomposition in Appendix Q.5 makes explicit. Although the first five candidates capture most eventual successes in all four groups, candidates six through ten still add 7.57.5–10.310.3 percentage points. This contribution also persists at 3232B in Medical. DeepSeek-R1 rises from 30.0%30.0\% at K=1K=1 to 67.7%67.7\% at K=5K=5 and 76.7%76.7\% at K=10K=10, while Qwen2.5 rises from 15.9%15.9\% to 41.4%41.4\% and 48.7%48.7\%. These trajectories motivate reporting both early susceptibility and final bounded-search coverage when evaluating one-sentence interventions.

Model rankings can reverse across tasks.

The full figures reveal differences that group averages alone obscure. In Medical, GPT-4.1 has lower final ASR (52.1%52.1\%) than its nano and mini variants (56.6%56.6\% and 56.9%56.9\%), whereas in Cyber it has higher ASR (82.8%82.8\% versus 51.2%51.2\% and 39.8%39.8\%). Likewise, DeepSeek-R1-7B is more susceptible than the 1414B and 3232B variants in Medical (93.7%93.7\% versus 70.6%70.6\% and 76.7%76.7\%), but less susceptible in Cyber (92.5%92.5\% versus 98.9%98.9\% and 99.3%99.3\%). Together with the clean-accuracy comparison in Section 4, these reversals show why stronger task performance or a larger model cannot substitute for evaluating decision stability under a supported qualification. The full curves locate this instability within the search process rather than reducing it to a single endpoint.

Cyber budget-curve construction and supplementary measurements.

The original Cyber evaluation stops at the first successful candidate, so matching its selected sentence to the fixed candidate ordering recovers the first-success position and retained belief. Together with the complete 3232B and Phi reasoning evaluations, the original responses determine 1055010550 of the 1055610556 curves directly. Six successful cases contain duplicate candidate text with ambiguous positions. For these six, we reused the original clean answer and candidate ordering and reevaluated the prefix until the first success, requiring seven candidate evaluations in total. The affected victims are GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.6-terra, DeepSeek-R1-7B/14B, and Qwen2.5-7B/14B. These six curves use the supplementary responses; all others use the original evaluations. Every model’s K=10K=10 ASR is unchanged, and the main-table confidence values and pooled belief-shift distributions retain their original responses.

Relating the curves to candidate selection.

Each budget uses a prefix of the same candidate ordering and retains an earlier success as the prefix grows. Consequently, additional search changes which inputs are reached, rather than replacing an earlier successful response with a more confident one. Appendix Q.5 derives the exact relationship between ASR increments and changes in retained signed belief. At K=1K=1, this policy evaluates the first query candidate; the zero-query selector in Table 2 instead chooses from the generated pool without victim feedback. Their comparison therefore involves both the selection policy and access to victim feedback, with the complete release procedures given in Appendix J.
